claims.text: The nanoparticles are initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The onset and progression of phase transitions are governed by an interplay between surface-energy reduction and atomic diffusion rates.
Nanoparticle size strongly influences the transition temperature and transition dynamics.
Compositional heterogeneity strongly influences the transition temperature and transition dynamics.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during controlled heating.
Smaller nanoparticles have higher surface-to-volume ratios.
Higher surface-energy contributions in smaller nanoparticles reduce their melting point.
Compositional heterogeneity creates localized variations in atomic diffusion rates.
Localized variations in diffusion rates affect the uniformity and progression of the phase transition.
Smaller FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than larger FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles under identical heating conditions.
Smaller FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will have a lower melting-onset temperature than larger FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles under identical heating conditions.
Compositionally heterogeneous nanoparticles will exhibit a broader phase-transition temperature range than compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
The broader transition range arises from staggered melting of regions having different local compositions.
The proposed mechanism applies to FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles between 5 and 50 nm under inert-atmosphere conditions.
The exact quantitative relationships among size, compositional heterogeneity, and phase-transition temperatures are not well defined.
Prior detailed studies of these relationships in the specific FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticle system are lacking.
